choices: Pricing below marginal cost to drive a rival out
Charging a low price initially to gain a critical mass of customers
Charging the highest price the market will bear
Keeping price below the monopoly level to prevent entry

stem: Penetration pricing is most useful when:
choices: The firm is a monopolist with no entrants
explain: Slide p. 41: useful when strong network effects are present.

stem: True or false: The main goal of penetration pricing is to drive an existing rival out of the market.
explain: False. That is predatory pricing. Penetration pricing aims to win customers and reach critical mass.

stem: True or false: Penetration pricing can include giving a product away for free.
explain: True. Free, or even paying users to try it, is the extreme form (Reading Quiz Q5).

stem: Which firm is most likely to use penetration pricing?
choices: A firm selling a commodity with no network
A new entrant facing an incumbent with strong network effects
A monopolist protected by a patent
An incumbent facing no threat of entry
explain: It is the entrant's tool for overcoming lock-in.

stem: Why can a firm afford to raise prices after a successful penetration pricing campaign?
choices: Once past critical mass, network effects keep users from leaving
explain: The network itself becomes the reason users stay.

stem: Facebook appears on the S18 slides under which pricing strategy?
explain: Slide p. 47: free to users, building the network.

stem: A new social media app is worth little to its first users because its value depends on how many others use it. Which strategy helps it overcome established platforms' network effects?
choices: Penetration pricing: a low price or free product to build a critical mass
Predatory pricing to drive out established platforms

stem: Yahoo! offered free auction listings to pull users from eBay and failed. What does this show?
choices: Penetration pricing does not always overcome a strong incumbent network
Auction markets have no network effects
explain: eBay's network and first-mover advantage were too strong.

stem: A payments app gives every new user $10 for signing up. Which strategy is this?
explain: Paying users to join is an extreme form of penetration pricing to reach critical mass.

stem: An established software monopolist lowers its price to discourage a startup from entering. A different startup gives its new product away free to attract users. Which is which?
choices: Monopolist: penetration pricing; startup: limit pricing
Monopolist: limit pricing; startup: penetration pricing
explain: Incumbent keeping entrants out = limit. Newcomer building a user base = penetration.

stem: A video game console maker sells consoles below cost at launch to grow its user base and attract game developers. Which concept explains the low console price?
choices: Penetration pricing to reach critical mass in a network market
explain: More players attract more developers and games, which attract more players: indirect network effects.

stem: Each user of a new network values it at $0.20 per other user. The price to join is $40. How many users does the network need before joining is worth the price (critical mass)?
explain: Value per user = 0.20 × n. Set equal to the price: 0.20n = 40, n = 200 users.

stem: Same network ($0.20 per other user). The firm uses penetration pricing and cuts the joining price to $10. What is the new critical mass?
explain: 0.20n = 10, n = 50 users. A lower price shrinks the critical mass the network has to reach.
